newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade slamms Croatia over refugee issue.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade slamms Croatia over refugee issue.

text.p: The Yugoslav government joined a chorus of Western states and accused Croatia on Thursday of not sticking to the letter of a peace deal allowing refugees to return home.

"Croatia is showing insufficient cooperation and readiness for consistent implementation of the Dayton-Paris agreement and the agreement on the normalisation of Yugoslav-Croatian relations," it said in a statement.

Under the accords, the Croatian government undertook to secure as soon as possible an unhindered and safe return of refugees, expelled and displaced persons who expressed the readiness to return to Croatia, the statement said.

It said Zagreb plegded to provide an agreement on resolving the refugee issue within six months of the signing of the agreement on normalising Yugoslav-Croatian relations, which took place last August.

The United States warned on Wednesday that it might back a delay in allowing Croatia to resume control of the U.N.-administered enclave of Eastern Slavonia unless Zagreb allowed exiled ethnic Serbs to return to their pre-war homes there.

A group of Western countries earlier protested to Zagreb over the issue to Croatia. The United States and its European allies have been angered by Croatia's stubborn refusal to permit 350,000 exiled ethnic Serbs to go back to Eastern Slavonia.
Rebel Serbs seized control of the region six years ago as the former Yugoslav federation broke up. The 1995 Dayton peace agreement which ended the fighting laid terms for its return to Croatia.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is expected to discuss the dispute, among others, when she meets Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in Zagreb on Saturday.
U.S. officials said Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic and his delegation were shaken by the lambasting from Washington.

Albright has reportedly threatened to deny Zagreb access to international lending and membership in NATO's Partnership for Peace organisation and other Western institutions unless it complies fully with the peace agreement.

Belgrade's criticism of Zagreb came only two days after they agreed to speed up the normalisation of relations following the 1991-95 war and set a mid-June target for agreement on restoring full road and rail traffic.
Granic and Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic met for the third time since the former Balkan foes signed a normalisation agreement in August 1996.
Milutinovic said the top Yugoslav priority was the return of Serb refugees who fled from central Croatia after Zagreb crushed their rebellion in 1995.

Granic said Zagreb did not question the right of all refugees to return to their homes but the process had to be agreed and organised. The return of refugees was not only a legal issue but also a political, economic and security question, he said.
